q-165280.name: Question 1
q-165280.problem: Given that $f(x,y)=2y-xy,$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
q-165280.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2-x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )+(2-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡\theta -{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

Given that f(x,y)=2y−xy, find ∂f∂θ, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
 2rsin⁡θ−rcos⁡θ
b
 r2(cos⁡θ+sin⁡(2θ))
c
2rcos⁡θ−r2cos⁡(2θ)
d
 r(sin⁡θ+cos⁡(2θ))
e
 cos⁡θ−r2sin⁡(2θ)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function f(x,y) with two independent variables r and θ, where x=rcos⁡θ and y=rsin⁡θ, we have

∂f∂θ=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂θ+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂θ=−∂f∂xrsin⁡θ+∂f∂yrcos⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=−y,∂f∂y=2−x

Writing the above results in terms of r and θ, we get

∂f∂x=−rsin⁡θ,∂f∂y=2−rcos⁡θ.

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get ∂f∂θ=(−rsin⁡θ)(−rsin⁡θ)+(2−rcos⁡θ)rcos⁡θ=r2sin2⁡θ+2rcos⁡θ−r2cos2⁡θ=r2(sin2⁡θ−cos2⁡θ)+2rcos⁡θ=−r2cos⁡(2θ)+2rcos⁡θ=2rcos⁡θ−r2cos⁡(2θ).

q-37196.name: Question 2
q-37196.problem: Given that $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y),$ find $\frac{∂g}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
q-37196.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $g(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r} & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂g}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x+y},\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }, \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r} & =(\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta })\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +(\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta })\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{1}{r}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-95115.name: Question 3
q-95115.problem: Given that $h(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
q-95115.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $h(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂h}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂h}{∂y}=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -(2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2r({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

q-95108.problem: Given that $p(x,y)=2x+{y}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂p}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $p(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂p}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂p}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂p}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂p}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂p}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $n$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂p}{∂x}=2,\,\frac{∂p}{∂y}=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂p}{∂x} & =2, \\ \frac{∂p}{∂y} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂p}{∂\theta } & =-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}

q-165281.problem: Given that $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+y,$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
q-165281.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{∂w}{∂y}=\frac{∂w}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta 
$$

$$

$$

$$

q-95137.problem: Given that $h(r,\theta )=r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1),$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
q-95137.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂h}{∂x}=\frac{∂h}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂h}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r}=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1,\,\frac{∂h}{∂\theta }=-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}

Question 7

Given that h(r,θ)=r(cos⁡θ−1), find ∂h∂x, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
−cos⁡θ
b
−sin⁡θ
c
1−sin⁡θ
d
sin⁡θ−cos⁡θ
e
1−cos⁡θ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

∂h∂x=∂h∂rcos⁡θ−1r∂h∂θsin⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of h with respect to r and θ:

∂h∂r=cos⁡θ−1,∂h∂θ=−rsin⁡θ

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

∂h∂x=(cos⁡θ−1)cos⁡θ−1r(−rsin⁡θ)sin⁡θ=cos2⁡θ−cos⁡θ+sin2⁡θ=1−cos⁡θ.

q-95135.problem: Given that $v(r,\theta )=r(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ),$ find $\frac{∂v}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
q-95135.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂v}{∂y}=\frac{∂v}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $v$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂r}=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ,\,\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }=-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

q-95001.problem: Given that $v(r,\theta )=r(2+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ),$ find $\frac{∂v}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
q-95001.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂v}{∂x}=\frac{∂v}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $v$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂r}=2+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }=-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂x} & =(2+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1.\end{aligned}
$$

q-95168.name: Question 11
q-95168.problem: Given that $g(x,y,z)={x}^{2}z+{z}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂g}{∂z},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
q-95168.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $g(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂z} & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂z}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂z}+\frac{∂g}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂g}{∂z}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂z}={x}^{2}+2z\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂z} & ={r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11

Given that g(x,y,z)=x2z+z2, find ∂g∂z, where (x,y,z) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ,z) are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.

a
r2cos2⁡θ+2z
b
r2sin2⁡θ+z
c
2rcos⁡2θ+2z
d
2rsin⁡2θ+z
e
cos2⁡θ+2rz
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function g(x,y,z) with three independent variables r,θ, and z, where x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ, and z=z, we have

∂g∂z=∂g∂x⋅∂x∂z+∂g∂y⋅∂y∂z+∂g∂z⋅∂z∂z=∂g∂z.

First, we find the partial derivatives of g with respect to z:

∂g∂z=x2+2z

Writing the above results in terms of r,θ, and z, we get

∂g∂z=r2cos2⁡θ+2z.

q-95170.name: Question 12
q-95170.problem: Given that $w(x,y,z)=x{z}^{4}+y,$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂r},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
q-95170.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $w(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r} & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂w}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r}+\frac{∂w}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂w}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x}={z}^{4},\,\frac{∂w}{∂y}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & ={z}^{4}, \\ \frac{∂w}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r} & =({z}^{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={z}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

q-95169.problem: Given that $h(x,y,z)=xyz,$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
q-95169.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $h(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂h}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂h}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂h}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x}=yz,\,\frac{∂h}{∂y}=xz\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =rz\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =rz\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$

$$

Given that h(x,y,z)=xyz, find ∂h∂θ, where (x,y,z) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ,z) are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.

a
r2z
b
2rzcos⁡2θ
c
rzcos2⁡θ
d
r2zcos⁡2θ
e
r2zsin⁡2θ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function h(x,y,z) with three independent variables r,θ, and z, where x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ, and z=z, we have

∂h∂θ=∂h∂x⋅∂x∂θ+∂h∂y⋅∂y∂θ+∂h∂z⋅∂z∂θ=−∂h∂xrsin⁡θ+∂h∂yrcos⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of h with respect to x and y:

∂h∂x=yz,∂h∂y=xz

Writing the above results in terms of r,θ, and z, we get

∂h∂x=rzsin⁡θ,∂h∂y=rzcos⁡θ.

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

∂h∂θ=−(rzsin⁡θ)rsin⁡θ+(rzcos⁡θ)rcos⁡θ=−r2zsin2⁡θ+r2zcos2⁡θ=r2z(cos2⁡θ−sin2⁡θ)=r2zcos⁡2θ.

q-95045.problem: Given that $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{3}+{z}^{4},$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂r},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
q-95045.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =3{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +(3{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2r{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +3{r}^{2}{sin}^{3}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

q-165285.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂z}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂z}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂z}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z}=2xyz\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z} & =2{r}^{2}z\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}z\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$
